subtitle: Learn about disability leadership, civil-rights milestones and Minnesota’s changing service history, set within the wider U.S. story, while recognizing that progress is not finished.
scope: For staff across DHS. This is a selected historical introduction, not a complete disability history, legal finding or current eligibility guide. Actual services, requests, complaints and policy decisions use their applicable requirements and responsible roles. Practice cases and private, unrecorded reflection are available; no one needs to disclose a disability or personal history. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
introTranscript: Disability history concerns who could participate, who made decisions and whose knowledge counted. Laws and services changed through organizing, testimony, litigation and public decisions. People with disabilities were participants and leaders in that work, not simply recipients of help. Minnesota’s history includes institutional-service reform, family advocacy and a growing emphasis on community life. National civil-rights milestones provide another part of the picture. This course examines selected events and the questions they raise for everyday DHS work. A law, court decision or institution closure is important, but it does not prove that every barrier disappeared. Read the sources in context, recognize the people who shaped change and distinguish historical accounts from current requirements. You may reflect privately or follow the practice learning cases at your own pace.

lessons.title: Ask whose account the history includes
lessons.summary: Read disability history through participation and decision power as well as laws and services.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a historical event from a claim about everyone’s experience.
objectives: Distinguish a historical event from a claim about everyone’s experience.
Identify whose perspective a historical account includes or leaves unclear.
Use a source’s time and purpose to qualify a conclusion without dismissing its value.
takeaways: Disability history includes people’s leadership and choices.
A selected source cannot represent every disability experience.
A historical account and a current requirement answer different questions.
lessons.statement: Ask who speaks, what the source shows and what it cannot establish.

intro.heading: Ask whose account the history includes
intro.body:
A history told only through the names of hospitals, officials and laws can leave people with disabilities out of their own story. Those institutions and laws matter, but so do decisions about ordinary life: education, work, relationships, communication and community participation. Look for who organized, testified, described an experience or challenged an assumption. History can reveal both a change in formal rules and the struggle to make that change meaningful.

In a practice DHS orientation display, Mina finds a timeline that lists a law’s signing and several Minnesota institution closures. The events deserve accurate attention. The draft describes people only as recipients of services. Mina asks which self-advocacy accounts and family-organizing records could show how people helped shape change, without presenting one account as the voice of every person with a disability.

Sources have different purposes. A participant’s recollection offers a perspective on experience; a court document supports a legal history; a government timeline organizes selected events. A person’s recollection should not be dismissed because it is not a statistical report, but it also cannot establish a population rate. A source written in 1982 cannot report a 1999 outcome that had not happened yet. Use each source for what its evidence and time support.

Historical records may contain terminology that is now disrespectful or outdated. Preserve original records and understand the wording in context; use respectful language in your own account rather than adopting an old label for a person today. You do not need to reproduce harmful words to learn from the event.

You may privately consider how your assumptions about help and agency affect the story you tell. Use Mina’s practice display if you prefer. No colleague needs to disclose a disability, institutional experience or family history to make the learning authentic. Actual records, services and policy decisions remain in their appropriate processes.

items.title: Participation is part of the story
items.body: A service timeline may accurately name facilities while omitting the people who spoke, organized and pursued changes. Mina can add sourced leadership without erasing institutions or laws. The richer account asks who influenced decisions rather than presenting public officials as the only actors.

items.title: Do not make one speaker universal
items.body: A self-advocate’s account can provide knowledge that a policy timeline does not contain. It is still a particular account with context. Preserve its value without expecting one person to summarize every disability, family, community or service experience.

items.title: Read historical language without adopting it
items.body: An archived source may use an obsolete term. You can identify the period and describe the subject respectfully in new prose while preserving the original. Updating your explanation is different from silently rewriting an original record or using its old wording to label people now.

tabs.label: Official events alone
tabs.body: Official milestones can establish dates and institutional decisions, but may not show who contributed or how a change was experienced. Mina should keep the dates and broaden the question with suitable accounts. Adding experience does not require inventing a cause or abandoning source accuracy.

tabs.label: A single story as a complete history
tabs.body: One vivid story can be meaningful and still leave other experiences unexamined. Treating it as everyone’s account may erase differences among people and periods. Identify who is speaking, what the account describes and which further perspectives would help answer the question.

tabs.label: Several appropriate sources
tabs.body: A timeline, participant transcript and relevant court history can answer connected but different questions. Compare them without treating them as interchangeable. State a supported event, identify participation and retain what remains unknown rather than declaring the entire history settled.

check.question: How should Mina strengthen the practice orientation display?
check.correct: Retain verified events, add suitable accounts of disability leadership and qualify each source’s period, perspective and limits.
wrong: Treat one story as the experience of every person with a disability.
Describe people only as recipients because laws are the whole history.
Use an archived label as the correct way to name a colleague today.
check.feedbackCorrect: The account keeps factual events and people’s agency together while preserving the limits of the sources.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One account cannot represent every person. Laws are important but do not exhaust organizing, experience or participation. Historical terminology belongs to its context and does not automatically become respectful current wording. Use several suitable sources without rewriting originals or labeling colleagues.

items.text: The source was presented in 1982.
The published transcript describes a California self-advocacy organization.
Whose leadership does the display include?
What can this historical document establish about its own period?
One speaker describes every disability experience.
A milestone proves all barriers ended.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Mina’s display lists laws and institutions but describes no self-advocacy or family participation.
scenario.prompt: Which revision makes the history more complete and accurate?
options: Remove every formal event and rely on one personal story.
Keep sourced milestones and add contextualized accounts of people’s leadership, with limits clear.
Ask a colleague to disclose a disability history as proof.
responses: That loses useful evidence and still cannot represent everyone.
This includes agency and formal events without a universal account.
Private disclosure is not required to build a sound sourced display.

lessons.transfer: Privately consider whose agency a familiar historical account includes, or use Mina’s display. No personal history needs to be entered or shared.

move.control: You can choose sources that show events, participation and limits.
move.failure: A timeline erases people’s agency or a single account becomes universal.
move.next: Ask who speaks and what kind of conclusion the source can support.

lessons.title: Understand Minnesota’s institutional-service history
lessons.summary: Describe selected Minnesota reforms without attributing every change to one ruling.
lessons.objective: Identify the 1972 Welsch litigation as part of Minnesota’s service history.
objectives: Identify the 1972 Welsch litigation as part of Minnesota’s service history.
Distinguish litigation, service development and later closure milestones.
Explain why a closure date does not establish the end of every barrier or every type of institution.
takeaways: Minnesota’s service changes involved several connected decisions and efforts.
An event’s sequence does not by itself prove a single cause.
A developmental-disability institution milestone has a specific scope.
lessons.statement: Keep the event, its context and its actual scope together.

image.caption: Five colleagues discuss information around a meeting table in an office.

intro.heading: Understand Minnesota’s institutional-service history
intro.body:
Minnesota’s disability-service history includes challenges to institutional conditions and the development of community-based supports. The Welsch lawsuit began in 1972 on behalf of residents with developmental disabilities. The Governor’s Council’s later account describes early concerns about staffing, medication, restraint and living conditions, followed by greater emphasis on community homes and the quality of support after discharge. This was an extended history, not one decision that immediately transformed every service.

The Council’s account identifies later settlements and final dismissal in 1989. It also expressly explains that no court order or settlement in the case required the closing of the state institutions. Litigation, home- and community-based waiver funding and public commitment to community services contributed to later changes. Do not turn a connected history into the unsupported claim that a single Welsch order closed every facility.

Selected milestones identify Faribault in 1998, Cambridge in 1999 and the last resident of a Minnesota state institution for people with developmental disabilities leaving Fergus Falls in 2000. That last statement has a defined population and service context. It is not a statement that every psychiatric, forensic, residential or other institution in Minnesota ceased to exist, or that every community-service barrier disappeared.

Mina’s practice timeline initially places a 1999 Supreme Court ruling immediately before the Minnesota milestones and implies the ruling alone caused all the closures. The earlier litigation and service work make that account incomplete. Sequence is not a sufficient causal explanation. A sound display keeps verified dates and identifies the different strands of reform without inventing a simple cause.

Historical understanding can sharpen today’s questions about choice, supports and implementation. It cannot determine a person’s current service eligibility or authorize changing a plan. Use the historical record with its limits, and use the actual current processes for present decisions.

items.title: Early and later questions differed
items.body: The Council account describes an early focus on institutional conditions and a later focus on community homes and support quality. Reading both prevents a simplistic story in which the only issue was a building’s location. People’s actual support and life opportunities remained important.

items.title: No universal closure order
items.body: Welsch was consequential, but the Council’s account does not say a court ordered every institution closed. The later outcome involved service financing and public decisions alongside litigation. Preserve that distinction when teaching history or drawing an analogy for a present policy.

items.title: Define the 2000 statement precisely
items.body: The milestone concerns the last resident of a Minnesota state institution for people with developmental disabilities. Removing that qualification would change the claim. It also says nothing by itself about whether each person’s later support met their goals or whether other forms of segregation continued.

tabs.label: One ruling explains everything
tabs.body: A one-ruling account can hide earlier organizing, funding and service work. It may also misstate what the ruling required. Mina should identify the multiple documented strands and retain uncertainty where the evidence does not establish their separate contributions.

tabs.label: A date proves the whole outcome
tabs.body: A closure date is a significant event, but it does not measure the quality of every subsequent service. Supports, choices and ordinary community opportunities need their own evidence. Do not dismiss the milestone; describe what it establishes and which outcome questions remain.

tabs.label: Contextualized milestones
tabs.body: The 1972 litigation, later settlement history and 1998–2000 developmental-disability milestones can be presented together with their scope. This makes the story more accurate and opens useful questions about how reforms were implemented without treating a timeline as a current service decision.

check.question: Which statement accurately describes the Minnesota milestones?
check.correct: They concern defined developmental-disability service changes within a longer history; they do not prove every type of institution closed or every barrier ended.
wrong: A Welsch order alone required every Minnesota institution to close immediately.
The 2000 milestone proves all psychiatric and forensic institutions disappeared.
Chronological order proves one 1999 ruling caused every earlier and later reform.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement preserves population, timing and the limits of what a milestone can establish.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The Council account explicitly does not describe a universal Welsch closure order. The 2000 event has a developmental-disability scope, not every type of institution. A sequence does not prove sole causation, especially when relevant work began earlier. Keep dates, context and outcome questions separate.

items.text: Welsch litigation began in 1972.
The 2000 milestone concerns developmental-disability state-institution residents.
How did service funding and implementation contribute?
What later support and choice did people experience?
Every kind of institution disappeared in 2000.
A single Welsch order required all the later closures.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Mina writes that one court ruling ended all institutional services in Minnesota. The sources describe a longer, narrower history.
options: Keep the simple claim because a timeline needs an easy ending.
Delete the milestones because their effects were not universal.
Describe the documented litigation, service work and defined milestones, without a universal closure or sole-cause claim.
responses: Simplicity cannot justify changing the scope of the record.
A bounded event still matters even when it does not establish every outcome.
This keeps the evidence and its historical context intact.

lessons.transfer: Use Mina’s timeline to distinguish one verified event, its scope and a later outcome question. The practice exercise may remain private and unrecorded.

move.control: You can preserve important history without stretching a claim beyond its evidence.
move.failure: A milestone becomes proof of universal closure, sole causation or complete access.
move.next: Keep the population, period and outcome question explicit.

lessons.title: Recognize advocacy and disability leadership
lessons.summary: Distinguish speaking for people from creating meaningful opportunities for their own participation.
lessons.objective: Identify family advocacy and self-advocacy as related but distinct historical contributions.
objectives: Identify family advocacy and self-advocacy as related but distinct historical contributions.
Use a self-advocate’s account without making it a universal community story.
Choose a practice participation approach that values a person’s own contribution and suitable supports.
takeaways: People with disabilities helped shape rights and services.
Family and professional knowledge do not replace every person’s own perspective.
Support can enable participation without transferring the whole voice or decision.
lessons.statement: Include people’s leadership, not only the help provided to them.

image.caption: Five colleagues discuss information around a meeting table in an office.

intro.heading: Recognize advocacy and disability leadership
intro.body:
Advocacy is not a single story. The Governor’s Council records a national parent-association conference in Minneapolis in September 1950, an event connected with the organization now known as The Arc. Family advocacy helped bring rights and services into public debate. That is an important contribution, but it should not be told as though families or professionals were the only people able to speak about disability.

The Council also publishes a transcript about Capitol People First, a California organization directed by people with developmental disabilities. Its members describe learning advocacy, being listened to, participating in public decisions and teaching peers. The transcript shows people as organizers and contributors. It is a particular historical account from California, not a claim that the organization was in Minnesota or that every person had the same experience.

In this example, during a DHS advisory meeting, Emmett wants to contribute a typed comment. The facilitator plans to ask a professional to summarize all participants’ preferences because spoken discussion is easier to schedule. Family and professional contributions may be valuable, but that convenience does not make Emmett’s own account irrelevant. A suitable contribution route can make room for typed input and the supports the person chooses, within the actual purpose and requirements of the meeting.

Do not confuse support with erasing agency. People can use assistance and still have perspectives, preferences and decisions of their own. Actual representation or decision authority follows its applicable arrangements; a history lesson cannot remove a court order or invent an authorized representative. Listen to the person through appropriate means without assuming that a diagnosis determines what they can contribute.

You may privately reflect on whether your idea of helping includes listening to the person or mainly deciding for them. Use Emmett’s example if you prefer. No colleague needs to become a spokesperson for every disability or provide a personal story for the class.

flashcards.back: Families organizing around rights, services and support; one important strand of disability history.
People with disabilities organizing, teaching and expressing their own interests and choices.
Appropriate assistance or a contribution route that helps a person take part without automatically replacing their account.
Actual authority to represent or decide follows its applicable arrangements; a course cannot invent it.

items.title: Value several forms of knowledge
items.body: An account can include a parent’s service experience, a person’s own goals and a professional’s technical knowledge without pretending they answer exactly the same question. Mina should identify whose account is presented. Treating one role as the complete voice of everyone affected can hide important differences.

items.title: Keep the historical location clear
items.body: Capitol People First provides a developed self-advocacy example preserved by a Minnesota public archive. The organization in that transcript is in California. A Minnesota archive does not turn every event it documents into a Minnesota event; location and source purpose remain part of accurate history.

items.title: Make contribution possible
items.body: Emmett’s typed comment can address the meeting question directly. Providing a suitable way to consider it is different from asking someone else to decide what Emmett probably thinks. Actual roles and supports should fit the task, with privacy and authority intact; a preferred route does not imply incapability.

tabs.label: Professionals speak for everyone
tabs.body: A professional may have relevant expertise but cannot automatically supply every person’s experience or preference. In the practice meeting, a convenience-based summary could omit what Emmett wants to say. Ask how the person can contribute appropriately instead of treating role expertise as a complete substitute.

tabs.label: Participation without needed support
tabs.body: Inviting someone to a meeting is not enough if the available contribution route excludes their stated way of communicating. Suitable support can matter. Do not require a person to prove independence by refusing help; examine what allows meaningful participation in the actual setting.

tabs.label: People contribute with appropriate support
tabs.body: The facilitator can make room for the typed comment and suitable assistance while respecting the meeting’s real purpose and procedures. The approach values agency and other knowledge together. It does not presume a diagnosis, change legal representation or make one participant the voice of every person with a disability.

check.question: What would better recognize Emmett’s participation in the practice meeting?
check.correct: Consider a suitable way for Emmett’s typed contribution and chosen support to inform the discussion, with actual roles and requirements preserved.
wrong: Ask the professional to decide what Emmett must want because it is quicker.
Require Emmett to speak without assistance to prove independence.
Treat Emmett’s comment as the preference of every person with a disability.
check.feedbackCorrect: The approach makes the person’s contribution possible without removing support, authority or individual variation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Convenience does not establish another person’s preference. Needing a contribution support is not a reason to erase a voice or demand unaided performance. One account cannot represent everyone. Value the relevant person’s own contribution alongside appropriate expertise and actual responsibilities.

items.text: The 1950 Minneapolis parent conference is part of family-advocacy history.
Capitol People First members describe teaching and policymaking in a California organization.
Create a suitable route for a typed contribution.
Ask which appropriate support would help the person take part.
A professional automatically knows every participant’s preference.
One self-advocate’s story represents every disability experience.

scenario.prompt: Which response values disability leadership and actual participation?

Replace the comment with a presumed preference.
Demand that Emmett speak without support before the comment counts.
responses: This values the person’s account without erasing other expertise or actual procedures.
A presumed account cannot replace the expressed contribution.

lessons.transfer: Privately examine what helping and listening mean to you, or compare the options in Emmett’s practice case. No disability disclosure or personal story is required.

move.control: You can include agency, appropriate supports and several kinds of knowledge.
move.failure: Help becomes deciding for people, or participation requires unsupported performance.
move.next: Ask what allows the person’s relevant contribution to be heard appropriately.

lessons.title: Place civil-rights laws in the historical sequence
lessons.summary: Distinguish selected federal milestones and the different settings they address.
lessons.objective: Identify Section 504 in the 1973 Rehabilitation Act and the ADA signing in 1990 as distinct milestones.
objectives: Identify Section 504 in the 1973 Rehabilitation Act and the ADA signing in 1990 as distinct milestones.
Distinguish the broad roles of education law, federally assisted programs and state/local-government disability rights.
Avoid treating a historical law’s passage as proof of complete implementation or a current case finding.
takeaways: Several laws address different parts of disability rights.
A legal milestone does not show that every barrier was removed.
Present questions need the applicable current requirements and responsible process.
lessons.statement: A date names an important event; the law’s scope and implementation still matter.

image.caption: Five colleagues discuss information around a meeting table in an office.

intro.heading: Place civil-rights laws in the historical sequence
intro.body:
The Rehabilitation Act of 1973, the education-law milestone of 1975 and the ADA signed on July 26, 1990 belong to a longer civil-rights history. These dates can help organize a selected timeline. They should not imply that no earlier advocacy occurred, that the laws cover identical settings or that access became complete on the day of passage. Disabled people and advocates worked to secure and use these protections.

Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act addresses disability discrimination in covered federally assisted or federally conducted programs and activities. The education law now called IDEA grew from the 1975 Education for All Handicapped Children Act. Its public-school responsibilities concern eligible children and appropriate education; it is not the eligibility rule for every adult human-service program. The ADA addresses a broader range of settings through different titles.

For state and local government programs, ADA Title II applies regardless of the entity’s size or receipt of federal funding. That differs from assuming that only a federally funded service has disability-rights responsibilities. Other ADA titles address other settings, including covered employment and private public accommodations. This overview helps identify which question to ask; it is not a full current compliance checklist or a substitute for the appropriate legal and policy guidance.

Mina’s practice exhibit originally describes the ADA as a building-access law and treats a ramp as the end of the story. Physical access matters, but public-service participation also involves communication, policies and access to programs. A more accurate display names civil rights and recognizes implementation work without declaring a legal finding about a particular office.

Use the timeline to connect events with their scope. Keep original historical names in context, without adopting outdated terminology for people today. Actual education, service, employment or complaint decisions need their current applicable processes; remembering a date does not complete those duties.

items.title: Different coverage questions
items.body: A public-school education question, an employment accommodation and a state service-access question may involve different legal provisions. A historical sequence should help the learner recognize those distinctions rather than apply one familiar law to every case. Consult the current appropriate process for an actual decision.

items.title: Building access is part of a wider picture
items.body: A ramp can support physical entry while an unusable communication method still blocks the service task. The ADA is a civil-rights law, not merely a building code. The overview does not decide whether a particular file violates a current rule, but it makes the participation question visible.

items.title: Passage and implementation are separate
items.body: A signing date is a verified event. Whether an affected person could later participate needs other evidence. Advocacy, enforcement and practical implementation continue as separate parts of the history; a milestone is neither meaningless nor proof of a finished outcome.

tabs.label: All laws are interchangeable
tabs.body: Treating the laws as one universal rule can confuse the setting, population and responsible process. The IDEA history does not create adult service eligibility, and Section 504 coverage should not erase ADA Title II responsibilities. Identify the actual setting before asking for current guidance.

tabs.label: A date proves completion
tabs.body: A date tells the learner when a milestone occurred, not whether every program implemented it effectively. Mina should retain the milestone while avoiding a final success claim. A later barrier can be examined through current requirements without denying the importance of the historical change.

tabs.label: Events with their scope
tabs.body: A timeline can identify 1973, 1975 and 1990, then briefly explain the different coverage questions. It introduces a useful framework for further inquiry. It does not certify compliance or authorize a learner to decide an actual legal, eligibility or accommodation question from memory alone.

check.question: Which explanation correctly distinguishes the selected milestones?
check.correct: Section 504, education law and the ADA have different histories and coverage questions; the timeline does not establish complete implementation or decide a current case.
wrong: The ADA covers only building ramps.
IDEA determines every adult human-service eligibility decision.
State services have disability-rights duties only if they receive federal funds.
check.feedbackCorrect: The explanation keeps legal milestones, scope and present decision responsibilities separate.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The ADA reaches beyond physical entry. IDEA’s education duties are not a universal adult-service eligibility rule. ADA Title II covers state/local-government activities regardless of federal funding. Use the applicable current requirements and responsible process rather than extending a historical fact into an unsupported case decision.

items.text: The ADA was signed July 26, 1990.
The 1975 education law is part of IDEA’s history.
ADA Title II addresses state and local government activities regardless of federal funding.
Section 504 concerns covered federally assisted or federally conducted programs and activities.
A ramp resolves every public-service access issue.
Knowing the signing date certifies compliance in every office.

lessons.title: Understand community integration and informed choice
lessons.summary: Connect the Olmstead milestone with appropriate supports, meaningful options and the person’s own decision.
lessons.objective: Describe the basic conditions in the Olmstead holding without turning them into an automatic placement rule.
objectives: Describe the basic conditions in the Olmstead holding without turning them into an automatic placement rule.
Distinguish a community address from meaningful opportunities for community participation.
Choose a practice response that supports informed choice without presuming a person’s preference or deciding an actual legal claim.
takeaways: Community integration concerns opportunities and participation, not only an address.
Informed choice needs usable information and attention to the person’s concerns.
Actual service and legal decisions require their applicable evidence, authority and process.
lessons.statement: Examine the person’s options and supports rather than deciding what a historical milestone must mean for them.

image.caption: Five colleagues discuss information around a meeting table in an office.

intro.heading: Understand community integration and informed choice
intro.body:
The Supreme Court’s 1999 Olmstead decision is an important part of disability-rights history. The Department of Justice explains the holding as a prohibition on unjustified segregation under ADA Title II. It identifies community-based services when they are appropriate, the affected people do not oppose them, and they can be reasonably accommodated considering available resources and the needs of others receiving disability services. These conditions do not authorize a learner to make a placement or legal decision from a short history lesson.

Community participation involves opportunities to live, work, receive services and spend time with people beyond a segregated setting. A community mailing address alone cannot show what those opportunities are like. The question is also whether suitable supports and meaningful choices make participation possible. A facility’s closure can be a historical milestone while the quality and availability of subsequent supports remain questions requiring evidence.

In this example, during a DHS learning case, Avery wants to understand a proposed community option but is concerned about overnight assistance and staying connected with friends. A staff member calls this resistance and suggests moving ahead because integration is always better. That response substitutes the staff member’s conclusion for Avery’s questions. Another staff member treats the initial concern as a final rejection and ends the discussion. That also overlooks the missing information Avery is requesting.

DOJ’s guidance emphasizes the opportunity for informed choice, including information about integrated options and attention to concerns. For the practice case, a useful next step is to clarify the available option, supports and unanswered questions through the responsible service process, then listen to Avery’s informed preference. This is neither pressure to choose a particular setting nor a promise that any requested service will automatically be available.

A real service review must use current applicable requirements and authorized roles. It cannot presume consent, dismiss needs because a building is in the community, or establish a legal defense from a general budget concern. Privately examine how your idea of helping relates to information, choice and support, or work entirely with Avery’s example.

Opportunities for participation in ordinary community life, rather than a conclusion based only on a setting’s address.
A decision made with usable information and attention to the person’s questions and concerns, through the appropriate process.
Services and assistance relevant to the person’s needs and participation; a history lesson does not determine an actual support plan.

items.title: A question is not automatically opposition
items.body: Avery asks about overnight assistance and relationships. Those questions identify information needed to understand the option. They do not by themselves establish informed consent or a final rejection. Clarify through the appropriate process and listen, rather than assigning a preference the person has not expressed.

items.title: An address does not explain daily life
items.body: A person may have a community address while the available schedule, transportation or supports limit meaningful participation. That possibility is a question to investigate, not a finding about every service. Ask what opportunities exist and what evidence would explain the person’s actual experience; do not use the location label as the whole answer.

items.title: Keep the holding and the decision separate
items.body: The historical decision establishes an important legal principle with conditions. An actual review may require professional, legal, policy and service evidence within responsible roles. A learner cannot declare every placement required or prohibited, presume a particular support is funded, or create an exception simply by recalling the word Olmstead.

tabs.label: Move ahead without the person’s informed choice
tabs.body: This approach treats a historical principle as permission to decide for Avery. It may leave important support questions unanswered and ignores the nonopposition condition. The staff member should seek appropriate information and listen to the person rather than use a milestone to pressure agreement.

tabs.label: End the discussion after the first concern
tabs.body: This approach avoids pressure but can also leave the person without the information requested. Avery’s question is not necessarily a final refusal. A suitable process can explain available options and address concerns while respecting the person’s choice; it should not make reluctance into a permanent assumption.

tabs.label: Support an informed decision through the actual process
tabs.body: This approach connects the proposed option, appropriate supports and Avery’s questions with the responsible service process. It respects choice and preserves the need for evidence and authority. It does not guarantee a specific benefit, decide a legal claim or treat the person as a symbol of historical progress.

check.question: How should staff respond to Avery’s questions in the practice learning case?
check.correct: Clarify the option and available supports through the responsible process, address unanswered concerns and listen to Avery’s informed preference.
wrong: Move ahead because a community address proves every need will be met.
Treat the first question about assistance as permanent opposition.
Promise any requested support without reviewing actual requirements or authority.
check.feedbackCorrect: This supports understanding and choice without presuming the outcome or creating service authority.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An address does not establish appropriate support or meaningful participation. A question about assistance is not automatically a final preference. Staff also cannot promise a service outside the applicable process or authority. Keep the person’s information needs and choice together with a supported, authorized review.

items.text: Olmstead addressed unjustified segregation under ADA Title II.
The holding includes appropriate services, nonopposition and reasonable accommodation with its stated considerations.
What supports and participation opportunities does the proposed option actually offer?
Address Avery’s unanswered concerns through the responsible service process.
A community address proves complete access and satisfaction.
A history learner can authorize any support requested.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Avery asks about overnight help and staying connected with friends before considering a community option.
scenario.prompt: Which response respects informed choice and the limits of this lesson?
options: Declare the move required because the option has a community address.
End the discussion because asking about help proves final opposition.
Use the responsible process to explain the option and supports, address concerns and hear Avery’s informed preference.
responses: The address and historical principle do not establish the person’s choice or every support need.
The concern identifies a question; it does not establish a permanent preference.
This supports the decision without presuming it or inventing service authority.

lessons.transfer: Privately consider how information and choice fit your understanding of help, or compare the practice responses for Avery. No personal service history or actual placement decision is required.

move.control: You can distinguish participation, information and choice from an address or a historical label.
move.failure: A milestone becomes pressure, a first concern becomes a final refusal, or an address becomes proof of complete support.
move.next: Keep the person’s questions, applicable evidence and authorized service process together.

intro.heading: Use history to ask better questions about present practice
intro.body:
Mina returns to the practice DHS orientation display with a different view of the assignment. A useful display can retain verified dates and explain what changed, while making room for disability leadership and the people’s experiences preserved in the sources. It can distinguish family advocacy, self-advocacy, litigation, service development and civil-rights laws without making any one strand the whole story. It can also acknowledge that later implementation needs its own evidence.

The revised display does not end with a claim that every barrier disappeared. It names the scope of selected Minnesota institution milestones, identifies the California location of the Capitol People First account, and separates a 1982 historical source from later events. The ADA signing and the Olmstead decision remain important milestones. Their inclusion does not certify every current practice or authorize a learner to decide a service, employment or legal question.

History can also make an everyday question more precise. If an invitation relies on one communication method, ask who can use that method and how suitable contributions will be considered. If a service proposal describes a community option, ask what information, supports and choices are available to the person. These are different present questions connected by participation and agency. They require current facts; the course does not show that a particular invitation or proposal is unlawful.

Use the appropriate work process when an actual issue needs action. The DHS Equity Policy gives agency responsibilities for relevant policies and practices; required tools, analysis, training and authorized decisions still apply. A personal reflection is also valuable when it changes how you understand people’s contributions and choices. You do not need to record or share that reflection, produce a live work document or disclose a disability to complete the learning.

For the final activity, use Mina’s invented display or a suitable, authorized draft without personal information. Identify one supported historical point, one question it helps you ask and what the present question would still need. This connects learning with care and curiosity without making the exercise a claim of compliance or a promise of a finished outcome.

flashcards.back: An event or perspective described with its source, period and appropriate scope.
A question about current opportunities, communication, choice or support that needs current information.
Further reading or private reflection that deepens understanding without requiring disclosure or a work product.
An action within the role’s actual authority and applicable process; course completion does not authorize or certify it.

items.title: Retain the event and improve the account
items.body: Mina need not delete the timeline to recognize its limits. She can keep a verified event, identify the people and scope, and remove an unsupported universal conclusion. The improvement preserves historical importance while making the account more accurate and useful for a first-time learner.

items.title: Ask a question without inventing a finding
items.body: A one-method invitation could raise a participation question, but history alone cannot establish who was excluded or why. Identify the method and what needs clarification. Do not manufacture a cause, group comparison or legal finding; seek the appropriate current evidence and responsible process for the actual issue.

items.title: Allow learning that is personal and private
items.body: Reflecting on whose choices you notice can change your understanding even before it produces an observable work result. That personal learning is worthwhile without compulsory disclosure. An actual request, complaint or policy duty still requires its real process; private reflection cannot replace it or be used as proof that it is complete.

tabs.label: A finished-progress story
tabs.body: This version gives a clear ending but turns milestones into evidence of every later outcome. It can obscure differences in populations, services and experience. Mina should preserve the event while identifying its scope and keeping present questions open where the historical source cannot answer them.

tabs.label: A history with no practical connection
tabs.body: This version lists dates accurately but leaves the learner unsure why participation and agency matter today. A practical connection can be a well-framed question rather than an invented outcome. Ask what the present issue needs without using the historical record as a current eligibility or compliance decision.

tabs.label: Accurate history with an appropriate next question
tabs.body: This version connects a sourced point with a current question about contribution, information or choice. It identifies what is known and what must still be checked through the actual process. The learner can practice privately with Mina’s display; a live case or personal history is not required.

check.question: Which final activity best connects this history with present understanding?
check.correct: Use the practice display or a suitable authorized draft to name a supported historical point, a present question and what current evidence or process is still needed.
wrong: Require everyone to disclose a personal disability story.
Certify present compliance from the dates in a timeline.
Publish a current service finding from a participant’s historical account alone.
check.feedbackCorrect: The activity preserves source limits, participation and a practical next question without imposing disclosure or deciding a live case.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Personal disclosure is not a condition of learning. Historical dates cannot certify current compliance, and one historical account cannot supply all evidence for a present service finding. Keep the exercise bounded while actual work follows its applicable responsibilities, evidence and authority.

items.text: Identify which population and period a closure milestone describes.
Keep the location and perspective of the self-advocacy transcript clear.
Private reflection can deepen understanding without being recorded.
An actual policy review still uses its applicable requirements and responsible roles.
Learners must disclose disability histories before finishing the course.
The timeline proves every current service practice is compliant.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Mina completes a sourced orientation display, then asks how its participation theme could inform a present invitation. No current participation data have been reviewed.
scenario.prompt: What is an appropriate next step?
options: Declare the invitation discriminatory and publish a finding from the historical timeline.
Ask which contribution routes the invitation offers and what current information is needed, using the appropriate process for any actual change.
Require colleagues to tell personal service stories before any question can be raised.
responses: The timeline cannot establish that present finding.
This turns historical understanding into a specific, bounded question without inventing an outcome.
Colleagues’ private histories are not a prerequisite for thoughtful inquiry.

lessons.transfer: Privately connect one supported historical point with a present question, or finish the practice display exercise. No disclosure, recorded reflection or live work product is required.

move.control: You can preserve source accuracy and use history to improve the questions you ask.
move.failure: Historical progress becomes automatic present compliance, or learning becomes compulsory personal disclosure.
move.next: Name the supported point, the current question and the evidence or responsible process it would need.

jobAid.subtitle: Keep disability leadership, historical scope and present responsibilities clear.
remember: Include people with disabilities as contributors and leaders, not only service recipients.
A selected account cannot represent every disability experience.
Distinguish a source’s period and purpose from the conclusion you want to draw.
A milestone does not establish complete access, sole causation or a current legal finding.
Historical learning and private reflection do not replace actual policy, service or reporting responsibilities.

sections.heading: Read the account
items: Who is speaking, and which perspective does the source contain?
What event, period, population and location can this source establish?
Which further accounts could add understanding without being treated as universal?
Preserve original historical records; use respectful language in your own explanation.

sections.heading: Keep the scope of selected milestones clear
items: Welsch litigation, service development and later closures are connected parts of a longer Minnesota history. Do not attribute every change to a single ruling.
The selected Faribault, Cambridge and Fergus Falls milestones concern developmental-disability institutional services; they do not establish the closure of every kind of institution.
Section 504, education law and ADA titles address different coverage questions. Use current guidance for an actual issue.
The Olmstead history involves appropriate services, nonopposition and reasonable accommodation with its stated considerations. A course cannot decide a placement or create service authority.

sections.heading: Connect understanding with a present question
items: Ask how people can contribute, what information they need and how their choices are considered.
Identify current evidence and the appropriate process rather than inferring a cause or finding from history alone.
Use practice cases or a suitable authorized draft. Personal disability disclosure and a live work product are not required.
Private, unrecorded reflection can have intrinsic value. Actual work still follows applicable responsibilities and authorized roles.

sources.title: Minnesota Governor’s Council on Developmental Disabilities: Parents start fighting for rights
sources.note: Historical account of the 1950 national parent conference in Minneapolis and family advocacy. This is one strand of history, not a replacement for self-advocates’ own accounts.

sources.title: Minnesota Governor’s Council on Developmental Disabilities: Welsch lawsuit 45th-anniversary account
sources.note: The Welsch 45th-anniversary section includes plaintiff counsel’s account of the 1972 filing, later settlements and 1989 dismissal, and distinguishes litigation from a court order requiring all institutions to close.

sources.title: Luther Granquist: A brief history of the Welsch case
sources.note: First-person plaintiff-counsel historical account presented in 1982. Relevant early chronology was checked; it is not a statement of current legal obligations or later closure dates.

sources.title: Minnesota Governor’s Council on Developmental Disabilities: Milestones since the ADA
sources.note: Historical Minnesota chronology for Faribault 1998, Cambridge 1999 and the last developmental-disability state-institution resident leaving Fergus Falls in 2000. This is not a claim that every kind of institution closed or all community barriers ended.

sources.title: Capitol People First: Published historical transcript
sources.note: Self-advocates’ accounts of an organization directed by people with developmental disabilities in California. It is not a Minnesota organization or a universal experience; the transcript, rather than the video, was checked.

sources.title: GovInfo: 35th anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act
sources.note: Supports the July 26, 1990 signing date and the role of disability advocates. Detailed current duties are examined through the relevant primary legal and agency guidance sources, not the article’s regulation-link labels.

sources.title: DOJ: Guide to disability rights laws
sources.note: Agency overview for Section 504, the 1975 education-law milestone and distinctions between ADA titles. Guidance is not itself a new statute or a complete current compliance determination.

sources.title: DOJ: Integration mandate and Olmstead statement
sources.note: Explains the 1999 holding, most-integrated-setting concept, appropriate services, nonopposition, reasonable accommodation and informed choice. The example does not adjudicate a claim or authorize a service reduction.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Current agency context for examining policies and practices through an equity lens. Required analysis, tools, training and authorized decisions still apply.
